1: The magnitude in three dimensions is Pythagoras extended by the third component. Writing a vector in unit-vector form makes its components explicit.
2: The vector from A to B is the difference of the position vectors, because you travel from the origin to A and then across to B. The distance formula is the magnitude of that vector.
3: A point on the line plus any multiple of the direction vector gives every point on the line, so t parametrises the line. Two points on the line give the direction.
4: The scalar product links the components with the angle between the vectors. If the product is zero the vectors are perpendicular, provided neither is the zero vector.
5: Parallel lines have proportional direction vectors. In three dimensions two lines can be neither parallel nor intersecting, and such lines are called skew.
